claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Its internal boundaries are prone to microcrack initiation under tensile stress.
An optimized multi-step heat treatment can induce controlled complexion transitions at internal lamellar boundaries.
Boundary complexion transitions can simultaneously improve tensile strength and room-temperature ductility.
Machine-learning guidance can identify annealing temperature, holding time, and cooling rate that promote beneficial boundary complexion transitions.
The proposed heat treatment can produce those transitions without altering the lamellar architecture.
The treatment must preserve the original phase composition and lamellar spacing.
The processing window must avoid phase decomposition and excessive grain growth.
Complexion-modified internal boundaries have enhanced interfacial cohesion.
Complexion-modified internal boundaries resist microcrack nucleation and propagation.
Heat-treatment-induced complexion transitions reduce interfacial energy.
Reduced interfacial energy and increased boundary cohesion mitigate microcrack initiation during deformation.
The boundary modifications distribute strain more uniformly across the microstructure.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength and ultimate tensile strength than the conventionally processed baseline.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation at failure than the conventionally processed baseline.
Conventional casting can produce an EHEA with a fine lamellar FCC/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and ductility.
Numerous internal boundaries in the conventional lamellar baseline cause local stress concentrations, microcrack nucleation, and catastrophic brittle failure.
Phase instability or significant microstructural coarsening may negate the proposed benefits.
The heat-treatment parameters needed for the proposed transitions may vary with alloy composition.
